assessment.nobel_worthiness: A conceptually clean and original discovery: time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect opened a whole class of band-structure topology that is now central to how electronic structure is classified and computed. The theory-plus-experiment pairing is the kind of result a first-principles materials theorist values, since symmetry-based classification and DFT screening of topological materials grew out of it.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the decisive theoretical prediction of the Z2 invariant and the spin Hall state in graphene-like systems; Molenkamp's group gave the first experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells after the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. Three-name credit is natural, though Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D generalisations by others are outside the supplied names, so some credit is left unallocated.
assessment.maturity: Two decades of independent confirmation, many material families and an established theoretical framework. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue; the 2016 prize honoured topological phase transitions, which raises a question of overlap but not of substance.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2016 topological-phases prize and exclusion of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu from the credited names (as I recall them; not independently verified).
Whether the experimental credit should rest on HgTe alone given later InAs/GaSb and 3D confirmations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is the principal modern framework for strongly correlated electrons, bridging model Hamiltonians and real materials via DFT+DMFT. It made the Mott transition and heavy-fermion and transition-metal-oxide physics quantitatively tractable. Its lasting impact on calculated spectra and material properties is large; I judge it from a field where I have direct technical familiarity, so I note a possible bias towards it.
assessment.attribution: The limit of infinite dimensions was introduced by Metzner and Vollhardt, with Mueller-Hartmann; the mapping to a self-consistent quantum impurity problem and the dynamical mean-field construction came from Georges and Kotliar. Metzner is not among the credited names, so a fair three-person split is not fully supportable; Georges, Kotliar and Vollhardt is the best available configuration but leaves real unresolved allocation.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with widespread independent use, cross-validation with experiment (ARPES, optics, neutron scattering) and extensions such as cluster DMFT and DFT+DMFT. Timing is appropriate; single-site and impurity-solver approximations are understood limits rather than doubts about the framework.
uncertainties: Omission of Metzner and Mueller-Hartmann from the credited names.
Quantitative predictivity for real materials depends on double-counting corrections and interaction parameters, which remain somewhat ad hoc.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions, then very large TMR with MgO barriers, underpins read heads and MRAM. The physics, spin-dependent tunnelling and symmetry-filtered coherent tunnelling, is clear and well supported by first-principles theory, and the technological impact is enormous and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera independently reported reproducible room-temperature TMR in 1995; Parkin and, separately, Yuasa and colleagues achieved the large MgO-based values. The supplied trio is credible, but Yuasa and the theorists of coherent tunnelling are absent, and the 2007 GMR prize may be seen as covering part of the same lineage.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and commercially validated for over fifteen years. Recognition is not premature; the main question is whether it is distinct enough from the 2007 GMR prize.
uncertainties: Exclusion of Yuasa and theorists of coherent tunnelling from the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of magic-angle flat bands and the observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene created the moire quantum materials field. It is a striking case where a continuum electronic-structure calculation predicted a specific angle that experiment then confirmed, and the field is now very broad.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the decisive theoretical prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the experimental discovery of the correlated states. A clean theory-experiment configuration, though the early-career experimentalists in the group and competing groups on related platforms raise credit questions.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups across graphene and TMD moire systems, but the interpretation of the superconducting mechanism and the relation to strong-correlation physics are still debated. Recognition is plausible but somewhat early.
uncertainties: Allocation of experimental credit within and beyond the Jarillo-Herrero group.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Current-induced spin-transfer torque made magnetisation dynamics controllable electrically and is the basis of STT-MRAM and spin-torque oscillators. It connects directly to the magnetisation dynamics and spin-transport theory I know well, and is original and technologically important.
assessment.attribution: The prediction is due to Berger and independently Slonczewski; Slonczewski is not among the credited names and, to my knowledge, is deceased, which complicates a fair allocation. Experimental demonstration is credited to Buhrman and Ralph and coworkers, with other groups also relevant.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed and commercially implemented. Recognition is timely, but the attribution issue is a genuine obstacle.
uncertainties: Slonczewski's absence and priority questions between Berger and Slonczewski.
Overlap with the spintronics lineage recognised in 2007.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED provides the architecture of leading superconducting quantum processors and demonstrates strong light-matter coupling in a solid-state setting. Its originality and impact on quantum technology are high, though the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is a close neighbour.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf form the core of the 2004 theory and experiment papers. I select the three that best balance experiment (Schoelkopf, Wallraff) and theory (Blais), leaving Girvin out, which is a debatable choice; credit among four people remains difficult.
assessment.maturity: Many independent demonstrations, but the route to fault-tolerant computing is incomplete. Recognition may be close in time to the 2025 prize.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits.
Four credited people against a three-laureate limit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices offer clean, tunable quantum simulators of Hubbard models, with the superfluid to Mott insulator transition a landmark. For a theorist of correlated electrons it is valuable as a controlled testbed of models that real materials cannot isolate.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and colleagues) proposed the Hubbard realisation; Greiner and Bloch observed the Mott transition in the laboratory. Cirac and Dalibard also contribute, so a three-person configuration omits important contributors.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely replicated, with quantum gas microscopes extending it further. It partially overlaps with earlier cold-atom prizes.
uncertainties: Five credited names against a three-laureate limit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magnetic skyrmions in chiral magnets and their emergent electrodynamics are an elegant example of topology in magnetism, with spin-torque effects at very low current densities. The physics is original and ties directly to topological spin textures that atomistic spin dynamics addresses.
assessment.attribution: Rosch provided the theoretical insight into the emergent fields and low-current motion; Pfleiderer's group observed the skyrmion lattice in MnSi, with Tokura's group providing real-space imaging in related materials. Credit also involves Bogdanov and the first authors of the experiments, not named here.
assessment.maturity: Well replicated, although applications such as racetrack memories remain unfulfilled, which argues that recognition may be premature.
uncertainties: Omission of Bogdanov and key experimental first authors.
Technological promise is not yet realised, which weakens the case for lasting impact.
